coursesData.courseName: Statistics and Machine Learning for Social Reform
coursesData.description: Social reform is an organized collective effort to restructure culturally accepted norms and improve various spheres of society often focusing on issues like inequality, poverty, education, labor rights, and family violence. Since the onset of industrialization in Europe, reform groups have employed statistical data to expose the social conditions they aspired to eradicate. Further urbanization, economic and population expansion, internal migration and the increasing public interest to social issues all make it essential today to understand statistics and machine learning from a sociological perspective. This course offers an overview of most popular statistical and machine learning methods including exploratory data analysis, model diagnostics, comparative and longitudinal modeling, dimensionality reduction and clustering techniques. With the use of R notebooks and log files, students will engage in hands-on data exploration and feature engineering, apply code, fit and critically evaluate models, and interpret the results through a sociological lens.

The Academic Speaking course develops students’ skills and confidence in speaking argumentatively on a variety of academic topics in the areas of Humanities, Business Studies and the Social Sciences. Students will be expected to undertake secondary research on their chosen topics and thereby develop their ability to use resources appropriately and ethically. Being engaged analytically and in-depth with their topics, students offer constructive criticism of one another’s speeches. Critical and analytical thinking will be emphasized at all times. Through regular speeches, analysis, and peer as well as instructor feedback on their research and ultimately on their topics, students will improve their language proficiency and ability to argue effectively and persuasively within an academic context, and to handle evidence and statistical data. Class activities will take the form of discussions and speeches.

This course provides a broad overview and synthesis of the issues and trends most relevant to the practice of professional nursing. Historical, contemporary and potential influences on professional nursing practice are reviewed. An emphasis on the unique and varied roles of nurses in today's interdisciplinary health care environment are examined within the context of individual, family, community, and global health. Characteristics and major changes in health care delivery systems (local and national) are discussed. Components of professional nursing values and core practice competencies are presented. The concept of an evidence-based approach to clinical practice is introduced. The nursing process is introduced and critical thinking strategies are outlined in the context of the nursing process.

coursesData.description:
This course enables students to deal with the academic reading and writing requirements of the program courses.
Course activities develop advanced-level reading ability by focusing on main ideas and specific information, by
recognizing lexical meaning from content areas in context, and by extensive training in paraphrasing, writing summaries,
responses, and an argumentative type of an essay that presents clear, well-researched arguments. Students will acquire
independent research skills, using online and print sources in a responsible and ethical manner so as to extend their
critical thinking ability within a piece of academic discourse including fiction and/or non-fiction literature. They will learn to
find and select relevant reading texts that provide information and interpretations that can be used to support their ideas
and provide evidence in their essays. Students will need to process and critically analyze that information before
incorporating it within their own arguments. A process-writing approach will be adopted, with greater emphasis on the
process of reading and writing and on drafts of the essay than on the final product.

coursesData.description: This course aims to present & study Additive Manufacturing (AM) technologies such as Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM), Stereolithography (SLA) and Selective Laser Melting (SLM), as well as an overview of AM and industry 4.0. The module includes a presentation of the different materials available for use with these technologies, such as photopolymer resins, plastic filaments for FDM printing and metal powders for metal AM, i.e., SLM. The production and properties of metal powders will be studied in detail. Topology optimization for 3D printing will be also covered in this module. Project-based learning is a major component in this course and therefore project assignments, lab experimentation and practical sessions will be used to develop student skills in designing for AM, critical thinking in reviewing models for AM and assessing the pros and cons of each applicable approach and technique. Formal assessment is carried out via 2 mini-projects (25 and 50%) and a final examination (25%).

coursesData.courseName: An Introduction to Comparative History:  The Eurasian Steppes and Great Plains of North America
coursesData.description:
This course will introduce the idea of comparative history. We will compare, and contrast, the history of two regions in different parts of the world, but with some similarities as well as differences in their histories. 
We will study the transformation of the steppes of Eurasia and Great Plains of North America between the 16th and 20th centuries. Large parts of these grasslands and the lives of their inhabitants  -- steppe nomads, such as Kazakhs, and Plains Indians, for example the Sioux -- were changed forever. Their lands were conquered and annexed by larger states: the Russian Empire, later the Soviet Union, and United States of America. 
The Russian and American states sponsored scientific studies of these lands, encouraged outsiders to settle or colonize them, and suppressed resistance. The settlers supported themselves partly by plowing up the land and growing crops. Their agricultural way of life partly replaced that of the native peoples who had relied more heavily on herding and hunting animals. The settlers reaped large harvests in good years, when the rains came, but experienced crises in years of drought. From the late nineteenth century there were attempts to develop more sustainable ways of farming and to conserve samples of the former natural environment of the grasslands. The changing ways of life in the grasslands were reflected in the cultures of the two societies.

coursesData.description: Heritage is a global matter. In the broadest sense, heritage includes both the tangible and intangible elements of cultures—languages, local history and archaeology, special technologies, traditional arts and performances, architecture, cultural practices and beliefs. Such diverse areas are enriched by incorporating insights from multiple disciplines, such as anthropology, archaeology, history, museum studies, political science, public policy, human geography, and others. Now more than ever, academics and governments are supporting approaches which foster greater collaboration when it comes to heritage. Public heritage aims to bring together multiple voices from researchers, institutions, and public stakeholders to ensure a greater appreciation for and understanding of heritage. Learning how to make heritage meaningful to the public is key to its protection and preservation. This course aims to provide students with the opportunity to bridge the gap between academics and the community to have meaningful conversations about shared heritage and what its role might be in today’s world. Students will connect with local or international institutions, cultivate skills for communicating heritage matters, and develop their own heritage-specific projects to present publicly either on a digital platform or through an in-person event.

Both dense urban centers and geographically dispersed ruins will be covered to examine interactions between the ‘powerful’ and ‘powerless’—and how this shaped world civilizations. coursesData.courseName: Beyond Common Sense: An Introduction to Paradox
coursesData.description:
A paradox is an argument that leads by apparently impeccable reasoning from premises that appear to be indisputably true to a conclusion that seems patently false. Solving a paradox therefore involves rejecting something that seems commonsensically indisputable (one of the premises, the reasoning or the denial of the conclusion).  That rejection can teach us something surprising and valuable about the topic of the paradoxical argument. 

Paradoxes covered may include Moore’s paradox (theory of knowledge and philosophy of language), the surprise exam paradox (theory of knowledge), the two-envelope paradox (decision theory) , the Cable Guy paradox (decision theory), the preface paradox (theory of knowledge), the lottery paradox (theory of knowledge and philosophy of probability) , the paradox of confirmation (philosophy of science), the Ship of Theseus (metaphysics), Thompson’s lamp (philosophy of physics), Achilles and the Tortoise (metaphysics), Newcombe’s choices (decision theory), the paradox of omnipotence (philosophy of religion), and the paradox of fiction (philosophy of literature).

coursesData.description: Biology for Medical Students I with Lab course focuses on the fundamental principles of molecular biology, cell biology, biochemistry and evolution. coursesData.courseName: Biology for Medical students II with Lab
coursesData.description: Biology for Medical Students II with Lab builds on NUSM102 to deepen understanding of the molecular logic of life. It integrates molecular and cellular biology, genetics, and biochemistry to explain how cells organize, communicate, proliferate, and die. Topics include membrane dynamics, vesicular trafficking, energy transduction, signaling networks, cytoskeletal organization, cell-cycle regulation, meiosis, apoptosis, and cellular interactions. The course emphasizes clinical and biotechnological relevance to health, disease, and therapy. A required laboratory component provides hands-on experience with modern biochemical, molecular, and cell-biological techniques, reinforcing theoretical concepts and developing experimental and analytical skills.

coursesData.courseName: Buddhism and science: view and meditation in the light of physics and neuroscience
coursesData.description:
Buddhism and science have developed models of reality based on empirical evidence and logic.
Eastern models of reality tend to be structured around mind, and one idealist current of Buddhist
thought even reduces matter to mind on the presupposition that mind alone exists (cittamātra).
Western scientific models, however, are inclined to privilege matter, to the extent that for extreme
proponents of scientific materialism mind has no place in a naturalistic account of the world. Given
this situation, the grounds on which Buddhism and science can meet are models of reality that do
not attempt to reduce mind and matter to each other. The acceptance of such a view inevitably leads
to the question of whether and, if yes, how mind and matter are capable of mutual interaction. Some
models of quantum physics suggest that consciousness, or the act of observation, may play a
fundamental role in determining the outcome of quantum events.

This course is meant to
provide a general introduction to the legal and ethical environment that affects individuals,
businesses, companies, governments and business transactions at local, regional and international
levels. This course will examine the law of international business and business ethics from the
practical, comparative and worldwide point of view. In addition to providing a general
introduction to the various countries’ legal system, this course will focus on specific legal topics
from international and comparative perspectives, such as contracts, corporations, capital markets,
Artificial Intellgience, IoT, fintech, patents and intellectual property and dispute settlement
across national borders.The globalization of business, along with greater advances in technology,
has increased the complexity of ethical decision making in business. An understanding of
business law and business ethics has thus become a crucial element in the organizational and
business environment. This course is also designed to provide an analysis and examination of
significant contemporary ethical issues and challenges existing throughout the professional
business arena.

coursesData.courseName: COVID-19: The sociocultural aspects of a pandemic
coursesData.description:
In addition to being a global medical pandemic, COVID-19 has done much to lay bare the ways in which we as human beings sharing a single planet view ourselves in terms of nation-states, races, ages, institutions, political ideologies, social classes, and, indeed, members of a shared humanity. While the pandemic has brought humanity together in some noteworthy ways, it has also laid bare many of the systemic inequalities that lay at the foundation of our global society.
This course will draw on the work of social scientists from a broad range of disciplinary backgrounds including sociologists, anthropologists, psychologists, political scientists, historians, economists, scholars of race and ethnicity, sex and gender, class and inequality, and a broad range of those committed to social justice. The aim of the course is to better understand the causes, impacts, and consequences of the COVID-19 pandemic from a social scientific perspective.

coursesData.description:
This course will look at China’s position in the world – through its history and since the
founding of the People’s Republic but with a heavy focus on developments and
conditions since the economic opening in 1978. The aim is for students to tackle some
of the big issues relating to China’s role in international politics and global affairs. Key
questions include: What impact have the political, economic and social currents in
Chinese history had on its contemporary foreign policies and relations? What has
China’s economic transformation meant for the global economy? What are China’s main
international relationships and how have their respective dynamics changed? In
particular, what has been the nature of the China-United States relationship since the
opening up of ties and diplomatic normalization in the 1970s? Are the global economy
and the international order now essentially a “great power” competition between China
and the US – and if so, what are the implications of such a framework for other
countries and regions including the rest of Asia (particularly East Asia and India),
Europe, Russia, the Middle East, Africa and what is called the Global South or the
Global Majority? How has the global emphasis on economic and national security risks
affected the outlook for the China-US relationship? Students should anticipate that the
course will cover significant current developments in the China-US and China-global
dynamic that will inevitably unfold during the semester. Topics for discussion in class
and tutorial may therefore hinge on keeping abreast of and analyzing these events.

coursesData.description: In the mid-20th century Hannah Arendt famously called citizenship “the right to have rights.” Citizenship turns humans into modern political subjects by enlisting them into demos and polity. This is why it stands at the center of political sociology. Citizenship has four dimensions: membership status, human rights, political participation, and civic identity. In this course we follow the recent developments in Eurasian citizenship and identify key forces shaping it: state-building, nationalism, migration and population transfers, foreign policy, patriarchy, economic transition, etc. We discuss how today we can keep to the ancient ideal of being a “good citizen” and a “good human” at the same time?

coursesData.description: This course introduces the fundamental principles of classical mechanics, including Newtonian mechanics, Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formulations, rigid body dynamics, oscillations, and central force motion. It provides the analytical foundation for advanced studies in physics and engineering

Classical mechanics I can be considered as a first course in theoretical physics. The course deals with the formulation of the laws of mechanics describing the motion of massive bodies under the presence of external forces. This formulation is related to the mathematical structure of space and time and requires several advanced mathematical tools. The relevant mathematical background is to be introduced during the course when required. The course covers Newton’s Laws, Reference frames, Gravitation, Oscillations, Central Motion, Lagrangian and Hamiltonian Dynamics. The topics learned in Classical Mechanics constitute the natural starting point for all other branches of theoretical physics including Astrophysics, Quantum Mechanics, Fluid Dynamics, Thermodynamics, Dynamical systems and Relativity.

coursesData.description: At the beginning of the 21st century the welfare state deserves more attention than ever before. The current economic crisis, accompanied by significant social and demographic challenges, has put welfare state reforms on the agenda of many North American, Western European, Latin American, East Asian and post-communist countries. The controversy surrounding the modern welfare state involves a large variety of issues: How can we define and analyze welfare states, what is social justice, what factors contributed to welfare state crisis, what actors are involved in the struggle for welfare reforms, what is the nature of the connection between the welfare state, the economy and the labor market, how do we account for cross-national differences of welfare state regimes, and what are the specific challenges those regimes face respectively? In this course, we will address these questions in order to gain some insight into the functioning of modern welfare states in different parts of the world and assess current government efforts of reforming them.

coursesData.description: During the course, the student will learn how high-level programming languages are translated into executable, low-level code. The course covers the complete process of: (1) Lexical analysis, which separates program text into keywords, identifiers and operators; (2) Parsing, which constructs an abstract tree representation (AST) of the program; (3) Type checking, which resolves overloaded names, and inserts implicit conversions; and (4) Lowering, which converts the resulting AST structures into an intermediate representation. The final part of the course discusses optimization through such means as detecting constants and eliminating redundant computations.

CAGD, which stands for Computer Aided Geometric Design, is the discipline concerned with the computational and geometric aspects of free-form curves, surfaces and volumes as they are used, for example, in CAD/CAM (Computer Aided Design / Computer Aided Manufacture), scientific visualization and computer graphics.
It is safe to say that CAD revolutionized modern day engineering. CAD allows for the easier development of products and product management integration and CAGD is its main pillar. Having thorough knowledge of the internal mathematical representations and modelling is a significant asset for every engineer that is willing to be involved in engineering projects.

coursesData.description: This course introduces Corpus Linguistics, one of the two most essential data gathering techniques in linguistics. A corpus allows us to directly observe language usage and evaluate it qualitatively and quantitatively. With a sufficiently large corpus, one can explore morpho-syntax and semantics while exclusively relying on context. Smaller corpora still provide a strong basis for subsequent elicitation. In this course, we will look at different types of corpora, how they can be created and used from existing materials or from scratch, and at different ways of searching these corpora.

coursesData.description: This one semester course, which is intended for students majoring in Computer Science, introduces students to the fundamental concepts of deep learning. The main themes of the course are benefits, properties and challenges of deep learning; introduction to machine learning and optimization; challenges and common approaches; logistics regression; gradient descent; perceptron learning; stochastic gradient descent; multi-layer perceptrons; non-linearity in ANNs; representational capacity; bias-variance dilemma; overfitting, generalization; regularization; convolutional neural networks; restricted Boltzmann Machines; deep recurrent networks and sequence learning; applications to pattern recognition from video data, speech recognition and natural language processing. Students will gain experience through assignments, with an emphasis on proper deep learning practices with appropriate applications.

The course provides an introduction to Discourse and Grammar – an interdisciplinary branch of language study, comprising research from typology, syntax, interactional linguistics, and cognitive science. Discourse and Grammar is an interdisciplinary framework that looks at the development of grammatical constructions from the point of view of language use. Discourse and Grammar is based on the assumption that speakers make functional choices at every level of structure and that, as such, grammatical constructions arise from the functions they serve for language users. The course will cover the two major direction of the interface between grammar and interaction: (1) how grammatical structures arise from fluid patterns of language use; (2) how stable structures of grammar provide templates for linguistic action.  The course acquaints the students with the main principles and notions of Discourse and Grammar, as well as with the different qualitative and quantitative methods used to carry out research in the discipline. The students practice applying these methods to the analysis of linguistic phenomena in Kazakh languages.  The forms of instruction include lectures, article presentations and discussions, and practical linguistic analysis.

coursesData.courseName: Economics of AI: Society, Work and Research
coursesData.description: This course examines how artificial intelligence changes work, research and the distribution of income, and asks what role humans retain when AI can perform much intellectual work. The course combines two activities. First, students learn economic ways of thinking about technology: tasks, substitutes and complements, scarcity, information and trust, and the ownership of productive assets. Second, students use current AI tools hands-on to test what they can and cannot do, comparing AI output with an external standard of correctness and documenting where human judgment adds value. The findings feed a discussion of social consequences: employment, wages, inequality, concentration of wealth and power, and policy responses. Assessment emphasizes oral presentation and defense of student work, and two closed-book exams. Students use freely available AI tools; no programming is required.

coursesData.description:
This course is about the economics of sustainability with an emphasis on policies that seek
to address environmental pollution and sustainability issues. We will connect
microeconomic theories with real world policy applications. The course begins with an
overview of microeconomic theories that are particularly relevant to sustainability policies;
then it moves on to the key topics in sustainability economics and policies. Particular
issues include market failure, externality, common goods and public goods, valuation of
non-market goods, environmental regulations, pollution, biodiversity, and economics of
climate change. The objective of this course is to develop an understanding of
sustainability issues from an economist’s point of view.

This seminar examines sustainable development from an economic perspective, with a focus on the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Students trace how the understanding of development has evolved, from growth-centred theories (Harrod, Solow) to broader approaches such as Sen’s capability perspective, and discuss why sustainable development requires interdisciplinary thinking. The seminar covers the shift from the Millennium Development Goals to the SDGs, ways of measuring growth and development (GDP, the Human Development Index, happiness indices), national and local SDG accounting, and trade-offs between goals. It then focuses on selected SDGs, including gender equality, reduced inequalities, life below water, strong institutions, and global partnerships.

The aim of this course is to present an overview of the relationship between economy and society: from the production of goods and services, to their distribution, and their consumption. Additionally, the course aims to provide students with a sociologically informed understanding of the structure of the economy more generally: networks, markets, and institutions.

coursesData.description: The aim of the course is an in-depth study of semantics, primarily with the help of empirical and in particular,  corpus and experimental methods. It aspires to explore the existing discussions, points of contention and different viewpoints on major semantic issues. During the course, students become familiar with the main theoretical issues of semantics, and through the study of selected research articles, form an idea of the various experimental research accounts of these issues. They test different research methods, conducting their own experiments related to the main course topics. They critically examine different research and identify points of contention and potential gaps. They formulate their own suggestions for further research, design and conduct an experiment. Thus, the outcome of the course is the design and realization of a full independent research project in semantics: the students must formulate the research question, choose the experimental method and tasks, develop the stimuli, upload the experiment on PCIbex online platform, conduct the experiment, download and process the results, interpret the data, and make a presentation including discussion of the results. The results of the experiment could potentially be developed into a qualitative paper if they are substantive and represent an advancement in the study of the respective field.

What is heritage, and why does it matter? This course introduces students to the interdisciplinary field of heritage studies, exploring how societies define, preserve, and contest physical and immaterial aspects of past and living cultures. We will explore tangible (e.g., artifacts, monuments), intangible (e.g., oral traditions, performance), and natural heritage (e.g., ecosystems, geologic formations) through global and Kazakhstani case studies. We will consider issues surrounding identity, power, and decolonization to help us understand who decides what should be preserved and what is ignored. We will also examine risks to heritage, including the impacts of conflict, excessive tourism, and climate change, but also the ways in which heritage is becoming more inclusive through digital methods and community inclusion. By the end of the course, students will possess a foundational understanding of the field of heritage studies and be able to analyze the complex political, ethical, and cultural facets present within these dialogs about the past and future of heritage.

This course focuses on the concepts of communication, therapeutic intervention, and decision-making as they relate to the nursing process. Techniques of assessment of the physical, psychological, and developmental dimensions of the individual are explored through a variety of learning strategies. Variations of expected findings based on influences such as age, social condition, and culture are discussed. Emphasis is placed on the therapeutic interventions of safety, hygiene and comfort, health assessment and health promotion.
This lab component is designed to provide lab/clinical-like experiences related to the theory provided in Foundations of Nursing Practice 1. Techniques used in the assessment of the physical, psychological and development dimensions of the individual within an acute care setting are demonstrated.

The focus is on the cognitive basis, scientific principles, and manipulative component of psychomotor skills used when providing nursing care which promotes, restores and maintains the health of the patient. During laboratory sessions, students will have the opportunity to practice simulated clinical skills. Nursing process, critical thinking and decision-making serve as the framework for acquisition of clinical psychomotor skills. Through active laboratory participation, the student will demonstrate self-direction as a learner.

coursesData.courseName: Fundamentals of Social and Cultural Data Science with Python
coursesData.department: Sociology and Anthropology, Sociology and Anthropology
coursesData.description: With the expansion of electronic sources such as cell phones, social media, and other online platforms, researches now have abundant data about almost every aspect of human behavior – from what we buy to what we believe in. Coupled with the mass digitalization of historical texts, artwork, and scattered family archives, this unfolding influx of data is ushering a revolution in methods of social and cultural analysis. This course provides a hands-on, non-technical introduction to the ideas and tools of Social and Cultural Data Science. This multidisciplinary research field sits at the intersection of social sciences, humanities, statistics, informatics and computing. We will explore key methods of classical supervised and unsupervised machine learning, text analysis, computer vision, and the basics of deep learning (ANN). Every week, we will learn how to apply advanced research methods to analyze real world social and “business” problems through hands-on data collection and analysis.

coursesData.courseName: Gender and Power in a Transnational World
coursesData.description: This course will introduce students to theory and praxis associated to diverse strands of transnational feminisms, such as third-world feminisms, postcolonial and decolonial feminisms, middle-eastern feminisms, political economy feminisms, woman of colour perspectives, gender and development (GAD), and social reproduction theories at the advanced undergraduate level. We will look focus on processes, meanings, practices, and expectations of gender, the intimate relations between gender and power, and at a lesser extent, the articulations between gender and sexuality, such as in the cases of sexual and reproductive health, and sexual and gender-based violence. We will explore how constructions of gender have been historically implicated in geopolitical projects. Through reading and analysing a variety of interdisciplinary materials, including several strands of feminist theory and empirical work, will build an analysis of how gender has historically been conceptualized in diverse contexts and what these conceptualizations mean for gender rights activism in a global and interconnected world. While we will look at gendered processes in the global north, we will focus our analysis in the majority of the world—the global south.

coursesData.description: This course is a one-semester course intended for undergraduate students. Students will gain a deep understanding of pivotal topics, including the intricacies and innovations of recent artificial intelligence architectures. The course will cover diverse generative models such as encoder-decoder architectures, contrastive learning, seq2seq models, attention/transformer mechanisms, diffusion models, and a variety of specialized loss functions. This comprehensive overview will equip students with a broad understanding of the key approaches in generative modeling. Students will engage in practical, hands-on projects utilizing real-world generative models to tackle contemporary challenges and applications, including computer vision, speech and natural language processing, graph mining, reinforcement learning, and trustworthy machine learning. In this course, students will be introduced to extensive, large-scale datasets pivotal to the field of Generative Artificial Intelligence. All practical components will be delivered using the Python programming language, leveraging the power and versatility of leading libraries, including TensorFlow, PyTorch, and Scikit-learn.

coursesData.description: German A2.2 for Exchange Students develops intermediate German language skills, focusing on improving speaking, listening, reading, and writing for everyday communication in academic and social contexts.

This course introduces complete beginners to German and builds the basic communication skills needed for everyday situations, in line with level A1 of the Common European Framework of Reference (CEFR). It follows the textbook Netzwerk neu A1.1. Students learn to greet people and introduce themselves, talk about countries, languages, hobbies, work, and family, and ask for and give directions. They also practice shopping and ordering food and drinks, telling the time, making appointments and phone calls, and talking about birthdays, invitations, and free-time activities. Grammar covers the basics: personal pronouns and verb conjugation (including haben and sein), definite and indefinite articles, negation, the accusative case, possessive articles, modal verbs, separable verbs, and word order in statements and questions. Pronunciation work and short notes on life in Germany, Austria, and Switzerland run through every unit. Audio, video, and exam-style practice develop all four skills: listening, reading, writing, and speaking.

coursesData.courseName: History of Islam Under Russian Rule
coursesData.department: History, Philosophy and Religious Studies, History, Philosophy and Religious Studies
coursesData.description: This course will focus on major transformations in the History of Islam in the Russian empire and the Soviet Union starting with the late 18th century to the present. Being under the rule of two empires, Russian and Soviet, Islamic institutions and practices in Inner Asia developed in particular ways and transformed in the course of the two centuries. We will engage in an in-depth study of how two successive rules influenced Muslim practices, scholars and laypeople at the everyday level. The weekly readings will be based around particular topics such as pilgrimage, Sufism, Muslim education, Islamic law and courts, women and family life, reform (jadidism) and reaction, law and society, religious administrations, Muslims in two world wars, Muslim and Soviet identity.

coursesData.description:
Commencing with the conquest of Constantinople by Mehmed II in 1453, HIST 371 provides a
comprehensive survey of the political, social, religious, and economic history of Ottoman Istanbul
through the early 20th century. The course tracks the evolution of the city from an imperial capital to a
modern metropolis, covering key themes such as the construction of the Ottoman urban landscape,
imperial ceremonies, neighborhood [mahalle] life, immigration, the status of religious minorities, gender
relations, justice administration, and the vibrant culture of public spaces like coffeehouses.
In addition to these themes, the course explores Istanbul’s role in international diplomacy and commerce,
as well as its manifold transformations from the classical age through the Tanzimat era and into the early
20th century. Designed as an undergraduate survey, the course combines lectures with class discussions.
Students will engage with selected primary and secondary sources to understand the texture of daily life,
urban dynamics, and the structural changes the city underwent over four centuries, rather than solely
focusing on abstract historiographical debates.

This lecture course examines how economists explain firms and the behavior of people within them, starting from the view that firms are a driving force of economic evolution and innovation (Schumpeter). Students critically compare standard approaches such as principal-agent theory and transaction cost economics with behavioral, developmental, and evolutionary perspectives, including the Carnegie School, organizational routines, corporate culture, and a naturalistic approach to the firm. A recurring theme is the motivational basis of organizational behavior: how intrinsic motivation can be crowded out by monetary incentives and control, and the roles of cognitive constraints, identity, trust, cooperation, and social learning.

The aim is to provide the student with the basic knowledge, theoretical and empirical, to understand and analyse the main economic problems of an economy at the aggregate level in the long run (economic growth) and in the short run (economic fluctuations) by means of the use of simple models. It begins with the study of the main determinants of income levels and the analysis of the international discrepancies in the levels of per capita income and productive capacity in the long run. Then it tackles the problem of fluctuations of the main macroeconomic variables around their respective long run values. In this context it studies the dynamics of inflation, interest rates and unemployment rates, explaining the economic policy means that can be used to stabilize the economy.

The aim of the Degree in Business Administration and Management is to produce professionals who can perform management, consultancy and evaluation tasks in organisations involved in production. These tasks may be carried out within the overall scope of the organisation or in any of its functional areas: production, human resources, financing, marketing, administration or accounting.
This subject aims to analyse international business issues from the perspective of the manager in charge of the firm’s international strategy. In doing so, the strategic management conceptual framework is used. Additionally, the peculiarities of international business in various fields, such as family firms, hospitality companies and emerging markets are explained.
Within this framework, the course is divided into two parts. The first one (comprising units 1-4) deals with the strategic management process for firm’s internationalisation. Thus, the main ideas to consider when making decisions on internationalisation are presented following the steps of this process: strategic analysis (country-, industry-, and firm-specific factors), strategy formulation (entry and competitive strategies), and strategy implementation (human resources, organisational structure, and strategic control).
The second part of the course (involving units 5 and 6) deals with international management in specific contexts. More precisely, unit 5 focuses on SMEs, family businesses, firms from Alicante province, and hotel chains. Finally, unit 6 analyses the strategies and key success factors in emerging markets, with a special emphasis on China and India.
Regarding the academic structure of the Degree in Business Administration and Management, the subject International Corporate Strategy and Management is included in two specialisation routes of the 4th year: Strategic Management and International Business. Moreover, this subject carries out an in-depth study of some concepts belonging to Strategic Business Management I and II (subjects of the 3rd year), applying them to an international context.

This course examines development as a long-term human process shaped by sur-
vival, cooperation, hierarchy, and technological change. Rather than treating de-
velopment as a purely economic or post-World War II policy project, the course
situates it within a broader narrative that begins with early human societies and ex-
tends to contemporary challenges such as climate change and artificial intelligence.
The course explores how power relations, inequality, institutions, and collective be-
liefs have shaped development outcomes across different historical periods and re-
gions. Drawing on insights from political economy, anthropology, history, and social theory, students analyze key moments such as the agricultural and industrial revolutions, colonialism, the emergence of modern development policies, and current debates on sustainability and technological transformation. Designed as a non-technical, discussion-oriented course, it encourages students to critically reflect on development as a contested and deeply human process rather than a linear path of progress.

In this course, we will study the basic concepts, tools and facts needed for the macroeconomic analysis of open economies, and to understand the functioning of international financial markets. We will start by relating the basic concepts of national income accounting and the balance of payments. Then we will examine the relationship between interest rates and exchange rates, which we will use for understanding the interaction of monetary policy and exchange rates. We will develop a framework to study the behavior of prices, interest rates, nominal and real exchange rates and output in the short and the long run. We will then apply this framework to analyze issues that are of current interest such as the causes and consequences of financial crises, relative merits of alternative exchange rate regimes and international capital flows.

coursesData.courseName: International Politics of the Korean Peninsula
coursesData.description: The Korean Peninsula is the last place where the Cold War politics remains dominant today: two Koreas remain divided with substantial hostility. However, the past quarter century witnessed fluctuating moods between long-standing adversaries. What can explain the variation in inter-Korean relations, and what can be said about the future of Korea? This course is designed to investigate the inter-Korean relations through different theories of IR and to provide historical knowledge about the case. The focus will be on changing strategies of two Koreas over time and the theoretical implications of Korean cases to the broader literature of conflict and international politics. This course is a writing intensive course, which requires a term paper no shorter than 5,000 words.

coursesData.description: The course will cover microeconomic aspects of international trade. It will introduce the standard models of the theory of international trade: The Ricardian model, where trade is driven by the comparative advantage based on technological differences across countries, and the Heckscher-Ohlin model, where comparative advantage and trade are determined by the cross-country differences in the endowments of the factors of production. history, and other social science research on global development. It will also introduce students to a diverse
set of conceptual and methodological research approaches in political science and international relations.

This course introduces the core concepts, tools, and workflows of data science, with a focus on its two leading programming languages, R and Python. Students first get an overview of what data science is, how projects move through the data science lifecycle (including the CRISP-DM framework), and which skills matter beyond the technical side: domain knowledge, problem formulation, and communicating results. The course then covers good programming practices such as reproducible workflows, literate programming with R Markdown and Jupyter notebooks, and writing clean, well-documented code. From there it builds hands-on skills step by step: basics of R and Python (objects, data types, vectors, lists, operators, conditions, loops, and functions), working with data and data infrastructure, data visualization (e.g., ggplot2 and seaborn), econometric approaches, and an introduction to machine learning.

coursesData.description: This course explores the geometry of curves and surfaces, blending concepts from calculus and linear algebra. It begins with the study of curves, covering their length, curvature, and reparametrization. The focus then shifts to surfaces, including their definitions, smoothness, and types such as quadric and ruled surfaces. Key topics include calculating lengths and curvatures on surfaces, examining isometries and conformal mappings, and understanding intrinsic properties through the second fundamental form and Gauss-Weingarten maps. Advanced topics address geodesics, Gaussian curvature, and significant theorems like Gauss' remarkable theorem, providing tools to analyze and solve geometric problems.

coursesData.description: This course offers broad introduction into emerging quantum technologies. The first part of the course covers past century of “the first quantum revolution”: the foundations, principles, and paradoxes of q.-(quantum) mechanics, from superposition and Schrodinger cats, to tunneling and interference of particles, uncertainty, entanglement, qubits, teleportation, etc. The second part of the course introduces “the second quantum revolution”, emerging in the last 25 years, where foundations of q.-mechanics is put to work in rapidly developing technologies. We discuss the major trends in q.-science, such as q.-information, q.-communication and cryptography, q.-computing and simulations, q.-metrology, sensing, and imaging. The state of the art and future challenges of q.-technologies will be illustrated with recent examples, such as extremely fast q.-computers, extremely precise q.-clocks, and extremely secure q.-communication lines. The course will conclude with brief discussion of our expectations for q.-technologies, public perceptions and market needs.

In this course we explore the nature of variation both within and across languages – how different ways of using language(s) can be meaningful and essential for our ever-shifting politics, cultures, and an increasingly interconnected world.

This course covers the fundamentals of solid-state physics spanning structural, binding, mechanical, vibrational, thermal, electrical, magnetic and optical properties of crystalline, defected and non-crystalline solids (metals, semiconductors and insulators). The properties and phenomena in solids are studied as a result of their interaction with external radiation, fields and particles. Take all the fundamentals of physics, including classical and quantum mechanics, electromagnetism, thermodynamics and statistical physics, and put them all together to study a piece of matter. Critical applications in material science, nanotechnology, solid-state devices, thermal and electrical energy transport & conversion, and materials characterization techniques will also be addressed. A grasp of fundamental and advanced principles and techniques in solid-state physics is very important in much of modern applied physical sciences, high-technology as well as fundamental research.

This course will examine a variety of topics in labor markets. First, we will develop theoretical
models of labor supply, labor demand and the interaction of the two. These models will then be
applied to understand issues such as wage determination, wage differentials, human capital
investment, migration and discrimination, unemployment and labor policies, and unions.

This course is designed to teach students how to use economic tools to analyze issues related to labor
markets such as wage determination, minimum wage, human capital investment, immigration, labor market
discrimination, and unemployment insurance. This course aims to help students improve their
understanding of labor markets and public policies by using economic theory and empirical analysis.

This course will introduce students to the economics of labor markets.  The first part of the course will focus on labor supply and labor demand, and some direct applications. Labor force participation rates of women, welfare and work incentives, earning gap across skill groups and technological progress, and fixed costs of employment are some of the topics that will be discussed in the context of this basic theory of supply and demand. The second part of the course will focus on a variety of labor market topics including human capital theory, household production, compensating wage differentials, quasi-fixed labor costs, job market signaling, labor mobility, and discrimination analysis.

This course primarily intends to introduce the students to a wide variety of materials and relevant theories. This course covers ferrous & non-ferrous materials and three other major categories of non-metallic materials namely ceramics, polymers and composite. Students will be introduced to the idea of production processes required for various materials. Different types of heat treatment processes such as annealing, normalizing, quenching, tempering, surface modification methods to improvise material properties further will be introduced.

Objects have substantially more power than we give them credit for. This idea lies at the heart of studies of ‘materiality’ – the two-way relationship between people and things. This course is about uncovering the social life of manmade materials that have shaped Eurasia through time, across millennia: clay, glass, metals, fibers, stone, paint, plastic, steel, concrete, and more. Anthropological and Archaeological case studies will be introduced to reveal those aspects of our social life that we often ignore and to discover the many relationships that materials hold to human culture.

The course provides an overview of various areas of mathematics and their applications in sustainability. It explores how mathematical methods can help address pressing global challenges, including climate change, biodiversity loss, resource scarcity, and social inequality.
Students will gain fundamental knowledge of optimization, game theory, stochastic processes, and differential equations, applying these concepts to real-world problems and models.
The course also develops students' ability to recognize the limitations of mathematical methods, identify innovative solutions, and communicate mathematical concepts to diverse audiences, including through interdisciplinary collaboration and public science communication.

This course provides a rigorous mathematical foundation for Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML). This course focuses on the nursing care of adults, including older adults, with acute and/or chronic illnesses. Students will be guided in critical thinking exercises and the use of therapeutic interventions and research findings in the management of adults. Nursing process, critical thinking, and decision-making serve as the framework for acquisition of knowledge for the management of patients. Societal and cultural influences will be emphasized.
During clinic, students will have the opportunity to practice clinical skills learned in the lab. The students’ ability to apply the nursing process, critical thinking, and decision-making serve as the framework for acquisition of clinical psychomotor skills. Common concepts of care will be emphasized, including societal and cultural influences.

coursesData.courseName: Medical-Surgical Nursing II: Complex Surgical Management and Clinical
coursesData.description:
The most valuable contribution to clinical care in nursing is the ongoing assessment and monitoring of patient status. Research on patient outcomes states that advanced nursing care is more likely to prevent failure to rescue and other poor outcomes.  This course is designed to provide the nurse with in depth competencies in the care of adults and older adults undergoing complex surgical procedures. Students will be guided in critical thinking exercises and the use of therapeutic interventions and research findings in the management of adults with acute and chronic illnesses that have received surgical intervention as part of their treatment plan. Emphasis is placed on using the nursing process for the prioritization and decision making processes of nursing care and the nursing responsibilities associated with translating, integrating and applying surgical management; evaluation of outcomes; and support for patients and families experiencing complex surgical problems.
The clinical nursing responsibilities include interpretation of diagnostic studies, medical/surgical patient management, evaluation of outcomes, health promotion, and support for individuals and families experiencing acute and complex health problems. This course includes application of cultural diversity awareness training to the nursing process. Clinical learning is focused on developing and refining the knowledge and skills to manage patient care as part of inter-professional teams. Clinical experiences are offered in acute care, critical care, and monitored units.

This course serves as an introduction to abstract algebra, the central language of modern mathematics. We systematically study the definition and properties of Groups, the most fundamental algebraic structure, and learn to rigorously analyze the symmetry and structure of mathematical objects. 
Topics include subgroups, cyclic groups, permutation groups, cosets, normal subgroups, and homomorphisms. In the latter part of the semester, we introduce the basic concepts of Rings and Fields. The primary goal is to transition students from computation-oriented mathematics to an axiomatic  approach, fostering abstract mathematical thinking.
Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:
1. Understand Algebraic Structures: Clearly define and explain core concepts of Group Theory, including groups, subgroups, normal subgroups, and quotient groups.
2. Prove and Apply Theorems: Rigorously prove fundamental theorems such as Lagrange's Theorem and the Isomorphism Theorems, andapply them  to concrete examples (integers, matrices, permutations).
3. Establish Foundations of Ring Theory: Understand the definitions of rings, ideals, and ring homomorphisms, and analyze the structural similarities  and differences between groups and rings.
4. Develop Abstract Reasoning: Cultivate mathematical rigor and abstract problem-solving skills by deriving theorems logically from axiomatic definitions.

coursesData.courseName: Museum space: collections, collectors and society
coursesData.description: The role and purpose of museums in contemporary society has been the subject of intense debate in recent decades. This course situates those discussions within a broader historical and theoretical framework, examining both the development of museums and the key concepts that shape current museum practice. Drawing on perspectives from art history, anthropology, and sociology students will engage critically with the question of what museums and collections are—and what they can become—in today’s world. Central to the course is the analysis of exhibitions as sites where societal values, identities, and norms are negotiated and communicated. Equally important is the critical study of collections and collectors: how collecting practices have been shaped by historical-political conjunctures, how they reflect shifting ideologies and hierarchies of value, and how individual collectors and institutional agendas have influenced what is preserved, displayed, or silenced. Special emphasis is placed on how (de)colonization, globalization, digital and AI transformation continue to reshape museum work and collecting strategies.

coursesData.description:
The human mind is the foundation of society and culture, and it is something we are intimately
acquainted with. But at the same time, its underlying nature is still shrouded in mystery and hard to
explain.
This course uses an interdisciplinary approach to explore the fascinating complexities of the mind. It
involves philosophical analysis, scientific investigation, and an awareness of history and the broader
social and moral implications of technology. A central issue is whether the mind is a computer. Can
computers display intelligence, creativity, and emotions? Can the computer model of the mind explain the
mysteries of consciousness and free will? Or do these mental phenomena require the existence of a
soul?
These issues are exciting not just because they are intellectually important, but also because to
understand the mind is to understand ourselves better. We will see how the ideas in this course can help
us become better thinkers, and improve our creativity and decision-making skills. We will also discuss
how science and technology can challenge our conception of the self, and how they might affect future
human evolution in radical ways.

coursesData.description: This course is concerned with the mathematical foundations of nonlinear continuum mechanics and theory of elasticity. Mathematically, the course is centered on a key concept of a tensor, frequently used in continuum mechanics. Mathematical preliminaries of the course are focused on tensor algebra. After dealing with mathematical preliminaries, the course will proceed to core topics of the course: kinematics of a deformable body, equilibrium and balance equations, and constitutive equations for hyperelastic materials. coursesData.description: The Optical Communications course provides an in-depth overview of fiber-optic communications for high bit-rate and high-throughput. The course provides a description of fiber-optic communication networks. Starting from an in-depth analysis of the devices that are fundamental part of the optical communication network, such as single mode optical fibers, fiber amplifiers, optical switches, filters, multiplexers, and photodetectors, the course aims to set the basis for assessment of network performance and for the consequent network design. New trends on signal modulations, applied to optical communication, will be exposed as an overview of future optical fibers networks.

coursesData.description: This course will trace the political, cultural, and intellectual history of Russia’s Orthodox Church over the 19th and 20th centuries. Through a close reading of primary sources and scholarly literature, it will examine the place of Orthodox Christianity in the reform, reaction and eventual collapse of the Tsarist regime. It will explore the opposition to radical socialism of Orthodox intellectuals, and the Christian utopian visions proposed by those same thinkers. The course will conclude with a study of the Orthodox Christian component of the Soviet and post-Soviet ideology of “Eurasianism.” Ultimately, the course will question whether Orthodox Christianity has served more to facilitate cooperation or to exacerbate divisions, both within Russia and in Russia’s relations with the world.

coursesData.courseName: PS: Introduction to Phonetics and Phonology
coursesData.description:
The course will cover the most fundamental areas and basic notions from the fields
of phonetics (i.e., the study of the sounds of speech) and phonology (i.e., the study
of the distribution of sounds in a language and the interactions between these
sounds). We will concentrate on the production of speech sounds (articulatory
phonetics), the transmission and physical properties of speech sounds (acoustic
phonetics) and the perception of speech sounds (auditory phonetics). We will learn
which sounds are possible in human languages in general and in English in
particular, and how they can be represented by means of the International Phonetic
Alphabet (IPA). We will also examine language-specific limitations on how sounds
can be combined in languages and discuss reasons why non-native speakers of a
language often have a foreign accent. Various factors and sources of speech
variation as well as regional and social accents of English will also be brought into
the limelight for discussion.
This course introduces the fundamentals of syntax and semantics, focusing on how linguistic structures relate to meaning through theoretical frameworks and problem-based analysis of language data.

This proseminar introduces students to theoretical linguistics through two core components of English grammar: syntax and semantics. Starting from the foundations of generative linguistics (linguistic competence, Universal Grammar, language acquisition, and parametric variation), students learn to analyze sentence structure using phrase-structure rules, constituency tests, and syntax trees. They then turn to the systematic study of meaning. The course follows Beck and Gergel's Contrasting English and German Grammar (2014) and combines weekly seminars with a tutorial.

This course is a necessary complement to the course on Sedimentology and Stratigraphy. It will cover the major groups of organisms preserved as macrofossils and microfossils in the geologic record. During the laboratory, the characteristic fossils for each time period will be treated. It will also illustrate the applications of paleontology to such important fields as paleoclimate reconstruction or petroleum exploration. The aims of this paleontology course are: (1) to introduce the students to the major groups of macrofossils and microfossils; (2) discuss the occurrence of fossils in the geologic record in terms of the origins and the evolution of life in general as well as in each major fossil group, as well as of the mass extinction events which have affected the planet.

coursesData.courseName: Peter the Great (1682-1725): First Emperor of Russia and “Father of the Fatherland”
coursesData.description:
In 1721 the Russian Senate granted tsar Peter the titles: “Emperor”; “the Great”; and “Father of the Fatherland”. 

Over his reign he transformed Russia’s image to emulate the states of western Europe. The most famous symbol is his new capital city of St Petersburg. He founded the city several hundred kilometers northwest of the old capital of Moscow and hired foreign architects to design it: St. Petersburg was built to impress. 

Peter carried out reforms in many areas: the armed forces; government and administration; the economy and society. He sent Russians to study abroad and promoted secular education inside Russia. He overhauled the relationship between the state and Russian Orthodox Church. Throughout his reign he pursued an imperial vision, fighting wars with Russia’s enemies - Sweden (successfully), the Ottoman Empire (unsuccessfully) - and promoted contacts further afield, including Central Asia. 

In this course we will examine the motivation behind Peter’s reforms, and assess whether he radically transformed Russia, or continued, with greater vigor, the policies of previous tsars. Students will have the opportunity to evaluate Peter’s reign on the basis of contemporary primary sources and to compare Peter’s new capital city with Kazakhstan’s new capital city of Astana.

coursesData.description: This course is labeled Philosophy AND Tragedy to reflect a dual concern with art and human life. First, we shall study the philosophy of the art of tragedy, examining the nature of tragic works as such and inquiring into the cognitive, emotional, moral, and political values distinctive of tragedy. Second, the course will look to tragedy to inform philosophical problems of human existence. These include such problems as human agency amid weakness of will; the conflict between moral and political values; the limits of rationality and the liberation of liminal experiences (such as religious and ritual ecstasy). Both our aims require a substantive engagement with tragedy; to that end, tragic works themselves will figure on the syllabus (e.g., by Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides, or perhaps other authors); we hope to include more contemporary literary works. Philosophers on the syllabus include, variously, Plato, Aristotle, Hume, Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, Nussbaum.

In this course we will consider some of the philosophical questions raised by law and legal systems. By the end of the semester, students will have a better understanding of some of the fundamental issues in the philosophy of law.

The field of Philosophy of Law encompasses numerous interpretations, and the constraints of a single semester compel professors to streamline content, focusing on select aspects of this multifaceted discipline. This course adopts a diachronic approach, offering a panoramic view of the many approaches to Philosophy of Law through history while emphasizing a core set of concepts fundamental to any robust philosophical conception of law. These key concepts include rule, obedience, punishment, justice, system, social contract, authority, sovereignty, principles, and rights, among others. The course structure is designed to simultaneously elucidate historical milestones and introduce pivotal concepts. These concepts serve not only as hermeneutical tools for understanding historical processes, but also as semantic units capable of transcending their original contexts and finding new interpretations in contemporary discourse. This dual approach is aimed at allowing students to grasp the historical development of philosophy of law while also engaging with its enduring conceptual frameworks in a modern context. Alongside seminal works by classical legal philosophers, the course adopts Raymond Wacks’ Understanding Jurisprudence as a core reference. This dual approach aims to provide necessary student guidance while prioritizing the study of original sources, a practice essential for stimulating autonomous intellectual inquiry.

coursesData.description:
This is a seminar about the economic governance of the European Union, studied from a political
economy perspective centred around questions like "how do the EU, its member states, and the
market relate to each other?", "how are economic policies decided, and by whom?", "why do
we get the economic policies we get?", and "who wins and who loses from the EU’s economic
policies?". The goal of the seminar is for students to (a) understand the main features of the EU’s
economic governance, (b) become familiar with main theoretical approaches used to study the
EU’s political economy, and (c) learn how to formulate and critically assess answers to political
economy questions about the EU’s economic governance. The weekly two-hour seminar will be
held in English and consists, broadly speaking, of two main parts. The first part will cover key
background elements of the EU’s political economy and an overview of theoretical approaches

used to study it. The second part will cover specific areas of economic policy (e.g., trade pol-
icy, monetary policy, industrial policy, competition policy, social policy) and evaluate academic

articles that study those policy fields.

coursesData.description: The objective of the course is to give Engineering students a working understanding of the salient features of polymeric materials, including structure, rheological properties and processing.  This course will cover the application and the analysis of several key processing operations for polymeric materials, namely extrusion, injection molding and calendering. Prior to this, the structure of polymeric materials and their rheological behavior and characterization will be reviewed, as they relate to processing. As part of the course, the students undertake an individual research project of computational (simulation and analysis of some polymer processing operation, possibly outside those covered in the class) or experimental (measurement of an important property of a polymer system, such as viscosity or glass transition temperature) nature. The final grade is the result of a final exam, a project and eight homework assignments. The course is open to Engineering students outside CHE, with demonstrated competence in Fluid Mechanics or Computational Methods. Such students might undertake a project related to polymer processing from the point of view of their particular discipline.

Is money the only thing in the world that motivates people? Don’t we really need a
regulatory mechanism like the state, or market is the miraculous mechanism to advance
human lives? Do we have to work to live a normal life? Do we have to be tough, aggressive,
and competitive to succeed in the neoliberal universe? What can we say about the culture
of the new economy? How do we rationalize and normalize the socio-economic
inequalities?
This advanced sociology seminar departs from questions like these. It aims to provide
students a general outlook on the workings of the current economy, i.e., deregulation,
neoliberalism, platform capitalism, sharing economy, and its highly contested outcomes
and costs like un- and under-employment, the shifting role of the state, poverty and
inequality, personality issues and identity under precarization through exploring
sociological and anthropological examples that are derived from the everyday life in
different parts of the World.

The course addresses project management in a general context and not specifically focusing on any one type of project such as construction or software projects. Moreover, an overview of Agile Project Management, Organization Structure and project management approaches are covered.

This course aims to examine the context, structure, people and important issues in
managing the public sector in contemporary China. The course provides students a basic
understanding of China’s public administration system and its reforms. Several very
important topics will be covered, including government structure and intergovernmental
relations, and how to manage public employees, administrative reforms, and key issues in
policy-making and implementation in contemporary China. This course encourages
students to conduct group project, which will allow students to learn public policy
analysis targeting real hot issues unfolding during China’s reform era. Sample policy
areas include environmental governance, e-governance, and diversity and equity issues in
public services. The newly emerged modes of public service delivery in China will also
be discussed.

In this course, students learn the basics of non-relativistic quantum mechanics. The course introduces the concept of the wave function, its interpretation, and covers the topics of potential wells, potential barriers, quantum harmonic oscillator, and the hydrogen atom. Next, a more formal approach to quantum mechanics is taken by introducing the postulates of quantum mechanics, quantum operators, Hilbert spaces, Heisenberg uncertainty principle, and time evolution. The course ends with topics covering the addition of angular momenta, spin, emergence of energy bands in periodic systems, and some basic aspects of many-body quantum mechanics, such as the indistinguishability of identical particles and electron orbitals in atoms.

coursesData.description: This course covers several widely used approximate methods of quantum mechanics: the variational method (including the Hartree-Fock approach), stationary and time-dependent perturbation theory, semiclassical approximation, and adiabatic approximation. In the framework of these methods some important applications will be considered, such as the fine structure of atomic energy levels, chemical bonding, theory of alpha-decay, selection rules for dipole transitions, Rabi oscillations, etc. Students will also learn the basics of quantum scattering theory. If time permits, some elements of relativistic quantum mechanics and/or the formalism of second quantization may be considered.

The course covers the principal methods of rock breakage used in mining including mechanical mining, drilling and blasting. Mechanical mining includes the rock cutting principles, cutting with picks and discs, effect of tool wear, impact breakage and ripping, assessment of rock cuttability and boreability, also, includes machine rock interaction and influence of parameters on mechanical rock breakage. Drilling includes the methods of drilling used in mining application. Blasting includes the chemistry of explosives and mechanics of explosive-rock interaction, selection of explosives, explosive charging techniques; and initiation and delay systems, blast design principles for surface and underground mines.

coursesData.courseName: Russian Literature in the Context of Eurasia
coursesData.description:
This course will study texts of Russian literature in the context of mastering and understanding the space of a huge country, of which Kazakhstan was once a part. Travel and wandering are one of the most important themes in Russian literature. Studying this topic allows one to better understand the mentality of the Russian person, and the deep philosophical and historical problems of Russian life.
The biography and creativity of such great writers as Alexander Pushkin, Leo Tolstoy, Fyodor Dostoevsky, Anton Chekhov, Andrey Platonov are connected with Kazakhstan and the space of Asia.

Introduction to Literary Studies explores key literary genres—poetry, drama, and narrative—through close reading of texts such as Shakespeare’s Macbeth and Shelley’s Frankenstein, while developing analytical and academic writing skills.

coursesData.courseName: Say What you Mean: Clarity, Precision, and Style in Academic Writing
coursesData.description:
In this course, students will build on the writing skills acquired in SHSS 150 and develop their voices in academic writing. They will learn to craft their own style of writing with an emphasis on clarity, audience, and purpose. Students will become familiar with the principles of strong and clear writing, e.g., cohesion, coherence, accuracy, and concision by reading selected texts across genres and time periods to identify how different writers express themselves while also effectively communicating with their audience. In analyzing the way these authors write, students will develop an eye for style and clarity, progressing from mere sentences to lengthier pieces of writing. Students will then be required to draw on this knowledge when producing their written works. This course is designed to appeal to students from any major who wish to focus on developing their writing voice.
This course satisfies the Core Curriculum Year 2 Writing & Communication requirement.

coursesData.courseName: Seminar: The International Relations of the Middle East: The Gaza War 2023-25 as a Case Study
coursesData.description: The October 7 attacks and the subsequent war in the Gaza Strip constitute a turning point in the International Relations of the Middle East. This Seminar will address the International Relations of the Middle East in the context of the Gaza War of 2023-2025. The Seminar is divided into two parts. In the first part, we will acquaint ourselves with relevant aspects of International Relations Theory aiming at understanding dynamics on both the regional and global level. In the second part, we will focus on in-depth case studies analysing strategies and policies of individual states and alliances. The course thus covers the drivers of foreign policy of the principal states involved on the regional and global level. The role of international organisations, such as the United Nations, will also be taken into account.

coursesData.courseName: Social Problems and Issues of Eurasia
coursesData.description: This is a survey course which aims to look into contemporary social problems in Eurasia with a sociological lens (i.e., using social theory and social science research).  Over the past two decades or so, societies in post-Soviet Eurasia  have been confronted with new and old social issues affecting well-being of diverse social groups. In addition, there have been shifts in public attitudes and perceptions of social problems and of how to address them. We will look into old and emerging issues and policy responses in the socioeconomic and political context of the region. Some of the issues of interest include rising inequality and polarization, changing demographics and family structure, health and gender issues, ethnic and race issues, migration, and environmental problems. This course explores major sociological theories of modern consumption. Since the early development of sociology, scholars have examined why people consume and with what consequences for society and the environment. Theories addressed in the course include status-driven consumption (Veblen), the influence of mass culture and ideology (Frankfurt School, Baudrillard), identity formation through consumption (consumer culture theories), social distinction (Bourdieu), political expression (politicized consumption), and acts of resistance (cultural studies). Students will critically engage with these perspectives to understand the complex nature of consumer behavior.

coursesData.description: Soft Matter is a term given to materials that are easily deformed or structurally altered due to thermal fluctuations or weak mechanical stresses. coursesData.description: This course will focus on the history of Soviet cinema and the representation of Soviet everyday life in films made between the 1920s and the early 1990s. Cinematic images immersed in a broad historical context will be our primary tool for defining and understanding the specifics of Soviet way of life. Drawing on various historical sources and critical analysis of films, we will discuss how cinema helps us to reconstruct the worldview of Soviet (wo)men and explain the causes of dramatic tension between the personal and the public in the Soviet discourse.

The program of the course consists of texts by Soviet female writers and poets written in Russian. The course aims to broaden the 20th-century literary canon which has traditionally focused more on male than female authors. Rather than analyzing “female images” in literature, we will talk about texts created by female writers and the writing strategies that they employed. During the course, we will address a variety of texts studying them within the Soviet cultural and historical context, with close reading being the primary method of analysis. The main aspects of the course will be the examination of several cases that illustrate different literary strategies of female writers.

This course explores the history of the Soviet Union through cinema, treating films both as historical documents and as interpreters of the past. By tracing the arc of Soviet history, from revolution to collapse, through cinema, the course examines how narratives and myths about the USSR were created, challenged, and remembered. With special attention to Central Asia and films by non-Russian directors — including both documentary and fiction films, and both more “artistic” productions and popular genre movies — students will learn to critically analyse film as a historical source and reflect on cinema’s role in shaping historical memory.
